title: Short Stuff: Venus de Milo
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Venus de Milo statue in the Louvre. Covers how the statue came to Paris in 1821 (donated by Louis XVIII) and its role in French national pride after Napoleon's plundering and England's acquisition of the Elgin Marbles. Discusses the mystery of the sculptor's identity, including a pedestal signature by Alexandros of Magnesia that was later lost, and the debate over whether the statue is classical or neoclassical, citing German archaeologist Adolf Furtwängler. Explores the identity of the figure (Aphrodite, Amphitrite, or an ordinary person) and the missing arms, including a found arm holding an apple tied to the Judgment of Paris myth, and Elizabeth Wayland Barber's theory that she is a woman spinning thread. Ends with a note on visiting the Louvre and a sponsor-style closing.

segments.title: Opening and history of the statue's arrival in Paris
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Venus de Milo and its donation to the Louvre by Louis XVIII in 1821. They discuss how the statue boosted French national pride after Napoleon's plundering and England's Elgin Marbles, and introduce art historian Andrew Stewart.

segments.title: Mystery of the sculptor and neoclassical debate
segments.summary: The hosts explain the statue's unknown identity and artist. They note it is not Venus the Roman goddess but Greek, possibly Aphrodite or Amphitrite, and discuss whether it is classical or neoclassical, citing Adolf Furtwängler. They mention a pedestal signature by Alexandros of Magnesia that was later lost.

segments.title: Missing arms and the apple theory
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the broken-off arms, the metal jewelry and possible paint once on the statue, and a found arm holding an apple. They connect the apple to the Judgment of Paris myth and its symbolism of choosing love, war, or politics.

segments.title: Spinning thread theory
segments.summary: The hosts describe Elizabeth Wayland Barber's argument that the statue shows a woman spinning thread, supported by 3D renderings, shoulder musculature, and the link between Aphrodite and spinning. They also mention a theory about a possible spinal condition and note it would be hard on the back.

segments.title: Visiting the Venus de Milo and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts encourage listeners to see the statue at the Louvre and close the episode with a brief note on the show's production by iHeartRadio.
